planting.note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chinese catalpa tolerates a wide range of soils once established and grows considerably smaller and more compact than the North American catalpa species.

directions: Chinese catalpa is a smaller, more refined relative of the native North American catalpas, typically topping out at 20-40 feet rather than the 60-70 feet common in Catalpa speciosa. In late spring it produces upright clusters of small, pale yellowish-white flowers heavily marked inside with purple and orange-yellow spotting, followed by the same long, slender, bean-like seed pods characteristic of the genus, though generally shorter than those of the American species. Native to central and eastern China, it has naturalized sparingly in parts of the eastern United States and is valued in cultivation for its compact size, heart-shaped leaves, and cold hardiness into zone 4. Give it an open, sunny site with room for its broad, rounded crown.

subcategory: fast-growing deciduous timber and shade tree

planting.note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; this species is bred and planted extensively in biomass and reforestation plantations in China and the southeastern US for its exceptionally rapid trunk growth. Remove seed capsules where naturalizing is a concern.

directions: Paulownia elongata is the species most widely selected for commercial fast-growth timber and biomass plantations in China and increasingly in the American South, prized for trunks that can reach harvestable diameter in under a decade. Large, velvety, heart-shaped leaves emerge after an early-spring show of upright panicles of pale lavender, foxglove-shaped flowers. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than Paulownia tomentosa but shares the same extraordinarily light, strong, warp-resistant wood prized in Asian woodworking. Like other paulownias it self-sows readily from wind-dispersed seed, so plant it only where volunteer seedlings can be managed.
sources: USDA National Agricultural Library — Paulownia species for biomass
Mississippi State University Extension — Paulownia as an alternative crop

planting.note: Plant seeds or container stock in spring in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; this cultivar comes reasonably true from open-pollinated seed and is favored over seedling chinaberry for its flattened, symmetrical, umbrella-shaped crown. Avoid planting near natural areas, as with the species.

directions: The Texas umbrella tree is a distinctive selection of chinaberry grown specifically for its tightly layered, flat-topped, umbrella-like crown of densely whorled branches rather than the loose, irregular habit of the wild species. Lilac-purple flower clusters in spring are followed by a notably lighter fruit set than typical chinaberry, which has made it the preferred form for shade planting around homes and livestock pens across Texas and the southern Plains for generations. It grows extremely quickly into a broad, flat-headed shade tree and tolerates heat, wind, and poor soil better than almost any other fast shade tree available. As with all chinaberry, the fruit is toxic if ingested and the species can naturalize aggressively, so plant with that in mind.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tree Identification

planting.note: Start fresh seed indoors in warm water (82-90°F) in late winter and move seedlings to a large, warm outdoor pond after water temperatures reliably exceed 75°F; this hybrid is re-created from controlled crosses each year rather than grown from stored stock, since the parent species do not persist as perennials outside the tropics.

directions: Victoria 'Longwood Hybrid' was created at Longwood Gardens in Pennsylvania in 1961 by crossing Victoria amazonica with the hardier Victoria cruziana, combining the Amazonian species' enormous leaf size with the Santa Cruz water platter's greater vigor and tolerance of cooler water. The cross flowers more reliably and grows more robustly than either parent in cultivation, which has made it the standard giant water lily relative grown in public water-garden displays across North America. As with the parent species, the night-opening flowers shift from white on the first evening to pink on the second as they trap and release beetle pollinators. Grow it as a warm-season annual from fresh seed each year outside the tropics, providing at least 100-150 square feet of open water surface for a mature plant.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society
Missouri Botanical Garden — Victoria cultivation notes

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in very well-drained, lean, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic soil in full sun; tree pincushion needs no phosphorus fertilizer and grows into a far larger, woodier specimen than the shrubbier pincushion proteas, so give it significantly more room to mature.

directions: Tree pincushion is the largest-growing species in its genus, developing over time into a gnarled, multi-stemmed small tree with thick, corky, fire-resistant bark rather than the rounded shrub form typical of most Leucospermum. Large, bright yellow, dome-shaped pincushion flowerheads open in late winter and spring on silvery-gray foliage, and the thick bark allows established plants to resprout after the periodic fires that shape its native habitat on the slopes of the Cape Peninsula. As with all Proteaceae, it requires sharp drainage and must never receive phosphorus-containing fertilizer. Its eventual tree-like stature makes it a long-term structural specimen rather than a quick-filling border shrub.

planting.note: Plant seeds soon after collection or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun in frost-free zone 10-12; Pacific Coast mahogany comes from seasonally dry tropical forest and tolerates drought and poor soil noticeably better than the larger-growing mahogany species.

directions: Pacific Coast mahogany is the smallest of the three commercially recognized mahogany species, native to the seasonally dry Pacific-slope forests of Mexico and Central America rather than the wetter forests favored by big-leaf mahogany. It typically reaches only 30-40 feet rather than the 100-plus feet possible for Swietenia macrophylla, making it a more manageable specimen or shade tree for smaller tropical and subtropical landscapes, while still producing the same reddish, close-grained, rot-resistant wood valued regionally for furniture and construction. Its origin in a markedly drier, more seasonal habitat gives it noticeably better drought tolerance than its larger relatives once established. Like the other mahoganies, it bears large, woody, five-valved seed capsules that split to release winged seeds.
sources: USDA Forest Service International Institute of Tropical Forestry

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring alongside a compatible nitrogen-fixing host plant, such as an Acacia species, in well-drained soil in full sun; Australian sandalwood is a root hemiparasite and establishes poorly without a nearby host, but it tolerates light frost and drought better than tropical sandalwood once established.

directions: This species forms root haustoria that tap a neighboring host plant's roots for water and nutrients even while photosynthesizing on its own, so it should be planted alongside a suitable host shrub or tree rather than alone. Native to the semi-arid woodlands and shrublands of southwestern Australia, it is the source of the historic Western Australian sandalwood industry, with its dense, fragrant heartwood harvested after several decades of growth for incense, carving, and essential oil. It is noticeably more tolerant of drought, poor soil, and occasional light frost than tropical Indian sandalwood, reflecting its origin in a drier, more temperate climate. As with other sandalwoods, meaningful heartwood development takes many years, so this is a long-term planting best suited to a dedicated agroforestry or specimen planting rather than a quick garden project.
sources: Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development, Western Australia

planting.note: Plant container stock after frost danger has passed in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in zone 10-12; Pink Ball Tree grows considerably taller than the related Tropical Hydrangea (Dombeya wallichii) and needs more overhead and root room to develop its eventual tree form.

directions: Pink Ball Tree is a fast-growing Madagascar native that develops into a true small tree up to 30 feet tall, distinctly taller and more upright than its shrubbier relative Dombeya wallichii. In winter it produces enormous, densely packed, rounded clusters of clear pink flowers that hang below the foliage like oversized pompoms, creating one of the showiest winter flowering displays among tropical trees. It has become especially popular as a specimen and street tree in Hawaii, where its height and more tree-like branching habit set it apart from the lower, more rounded form of the Tropical Hydrangea already common in frost-free gardens. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain a strong branch structure as the tree matures, and protect young plants from any cold exposure.
